title: Burnout, Grief & Building a Business That Holds You Too
guestBio: Anabelle Elya is the founder of The Digital Doula, where she helps service-based entrepreneurs build smarter sales systems, CRM automation, and business operations. She began her career as a birth doula after investing her last $700 in training, and the human-centered skills she developed there now shape the way she guides business owners through change. Her own journey through burnout, a frightening pregnancy, and caregiving loss became the foundation for everything she teaches about sustainable business design.
excerpt: Anabelle Elya invested her last $700 in doula training, built a business she loved, and then watched burnout and a terrifying pregnancy diagnosis force her to rebuild from scratch — twice. In Episode 85, she and Aimee unpack what it really costs to be the person holding everything together, and what becomes possible when you stop. This is the conversation every entrepreneur who has confused capacity with worth needs to hear.
metaDescription: Anabelle Elya on burnout, grief, and building sustainable business systems that support the person running them. Episode 85 of The Manage Her®.
keyTakeaways: Earning more money does not automatically relieve the pressure of an unsustainable business model — if the structure is broken, a bigger revenue number just means more of the same exhaustion at a higher volume.

The skills developed in caregiving work — reading a room, holding space, navigating fear — translate directly into sales and leadership, and the people who dismiss that crossover are leaving real competitive advantage on the table.
A one-week task audit, where you honestly track what energizes you and what drains you, can surface the hidden costs your business is charging against your wellbeing every single day.
When delegating a task brings up anxiety or resistance, it is rarely about the task itself — it is almost always a question about identity and what you believe your value is without that work.
Automation and systems are not shortcuts for lazy operators; they are the structural support that protects space for creativity, deep client work, and the people you love outside of work hours.
Grief and caregiving do not pause for your business calendar, and the entrepreneurs who build flexibility into their operations before a crisis are the ones who survive one when it arrives.
Separating your worth from how much you can carry is not a mindset shift you make once — it is a practice you return to every time your business grows and the temptation to do more creeps back in.

pullQuotes.text: Burnout is not a badge. It is not proof that you worked hard enough. It is a signal that the structure you built was never designed to hold a human life.
I was building systems that gave my clients breathing room while I had none. At some point you have to look at that honestly.
When handing off a task feels threatening, the question isn't really about the task. It's about who you think you are without it.
The business has to support the person running it. If it doesn't, you're not building an asset — you're building a cage.
That $700 was the last money I had. And it was the most honest investment I ever made in myself.

quiz.title: What's Actually Keeping You at the Center of Everything?
quiz.description: This isn't a quiz about how productive you are. It's a mirror. Answer honestly — not as the entrepreneur you think you should be, but as the one you actually are right now. Your result will tell you something true about how you're relating to your work, your worth, and your capacity for change.

A.name: The Devoted Carrier
A.description: You show up for everyone, and you do it well — but somewhere along the way, doing everything became the way you proved you belonged. You're not just running your business; you're holding it together by sheer force of will, and part of you knows that's not sustainable. The work you love has started to cost you more than it should, and the hardest thing to admit is that some of what you're carrying, you chose. This episode will give you language for what you've been feeling and a concrete place to start putting things down.

B.name: The Quiet Rebuilder
B.description: You've already been through something that changed you — a season of loss, a health scare, a period when the business had to wait — and you came back different. You're building again, but more carefully this time, and you're not entirely sure you trust the new version of success you're reaching for. Anabelle's story will feel like a conversation with someone who gets it, not just the ambition but the grief that restructured it.

C.name: The Systems Seeker
C.description: You know something has to change structurally, and you're smart enough to know that hustle is not a long-term strategy. You've been looking for permission to build the business differently — not just more efficiently, but in a way that actually supports your life. This episode is both the permission and the roadmap, from someone who learned the hard way that systems aren't a luxury — they're the architecture of a business that can survive real life.

D.name: The Identity Integrator
D.description: You've started to notice that who you are and what you do have gotten uncomfortably tangled together. When someone asks you to delegate, something in you resists — not because the task is critical, but because you're not sure who you are without it. You're ready to ask the deeper question underneath the to-do list. This episode will meet you exactly there, in the space between productivity and personhood, and offer something more honest than another framework.

questions.question: When you imagine handing off a task you've always handled yourself, what comes up first?

options.text: Guilt — like I'd be letting people down or admitting I can't cope.
Relief mixed with grief — I've wanted to let go but I'm not sure who I am without it.
Practical anxiety — I just need to find the right system before I trust someone else with it.
A quiet identity question — that task has been part of how I define my value.

questions.question: When your business had a really good revenue month, what did you feel?

options.text: Proud but immediately pressured to match or beat it next month.
Grateful but cautious — I've learned that numbers don't tell the whole story.
Curious about what systems made it work so I could replicate it reliably.
A little unsettled — I wasn't sure if the success matched how I actually felt inside.

questions.question: How do you typically respond when life demands more of you than your business schedule allows?

options.text: I push through and handle both — rest feels irresponsible when things are busy.
I've learned to step back, but it took a hard lesson I wouldn't wish on anyone.
I look at what I can automate or batch so I can protect the personal space I need.
I struggle with it — my sense of self is so tied to being productive that stepping back feels like disappearing.

questions.question: If you did a one-week audit of your tasks, what do you think it would reveal?

options.text: That I'm doing far too much that belongs to someone else, but I haven't stopped because I think I should be able to handle it.
That my priorities have shifted and my task list hasn't caught up with who I'm becoming.
Specific inefficiencies I've been meaning to fix — I'd find it genuinely useful data.
That some of my busiest work is also the work I use to avoid deeper questions about direction.

questions.question: What does the word 'sustainable' mean to you in the context of your business?

options.text: Honestly? I've been telling myself the current pace is sustainable when I know it isn't.
Something I'm actively rebuilding toward, having learned what unsustainable actually costs.
A concrete goal with measurable outcomes — I want systems that can run without me at the center.
A way of working that feels like me — aligned with my values, not just my capacity.

questions.question: When you think about the question 'what are you still doing because you believe everything depends on you?' — what's your honest gut response?

options.text: Too much. And I know it. But stopping feels more dangerous than continuing.
Less than I used to — hard seasons taught me that things don't actually fall apart when I rest.
I want to answer it with a system redesign — give me the audit and I'll start there.
It makes me want to cry a little, because the honest answer is tied to something about who I think I have to be.

content:
There is a version of success that looks exactly right from the outside and is quietly destroying you from the inside. More clients. More revenue. More proof that you can handle it. And underneath all of it, a question you are too tired to ask: what happens to this business if I stop being the one holding everything together?

That is the question Anabelle Elya had to answer — not theoretically, but in real time, during a pregnancy that brought a terrifying diagnosis, during a period of caregiving and grief that didn't pause for her calendar, and during the slow, honest reckoning of rebuilding a business that had been designed around her capacity to endure rather than her capacity to live.

The $700 Decision That Started Everything

Anabelle didn't come from entrepreneurship. She came from healthcare, from a growing frustration that the system she worked inside wasn't built to truly support people through the most vulnerable moments of their lives. So she left. With her last $700, she enrolled in doula training — not as a calculated career pivot, but as an act of faith in work that felt meaningful.

What she found in that training shaped everything that came after. Birth work is not soft work. It requires you to read a room at 3 a.m. when fear is high and language falls short. It asks you to hold space for outcomes you can't control while keeping the person in front of you grounded in the present moment. It demands a particular kind of leadership — quiet, steady, attentive — that has nothing to do with being the loudest voice and everything to do with being the most present one.

Those skills followed her into every room she walked into after. Into sales conversations where the real objection is never the one being spoken. Into client relationships where trust is built or broken in the margins. Into leadership, where the most important thing you can sometimes do is stop talking and listen.

When Success Becomes the Problem

Here is what nobody tells you about building something that works: it can still be unsustainable. Anabelle grew her consulting practice, added services, brought in revenue — and discovered that earning more had not actually reduced the pressure she was under. It had just given the pressure a larger surface area.

She was, she realized, building systems that gave her clients breathing room while she had none. The irony was not lost on her. She was the product of her own unexamined blind spot. And the answer wasn't to work harder to keep up — it was to change the structure of the offer entirely.

That is not a comfortable conversation to have with yourself. Changing what you sell means confronting what you built. It means admitting that the version of your business that got you here is not the version that will sustain you going forward. And it means tolerating the discomfort of transition before the new model has proven itself.

What a Frightening Diagnosis Taught Her About Control

The most honest parts of this conversation happen in the middle, when Anabelle describes what it was like to face a serious diagnosis during pregnancy and have to step away from work that had become, in more ways than she had admitted, tied to her identity.

You work hard enough for long enough, and the work stops being something you do and becomes something you are. So when it's taken from you — by a body that needs rest, by a family that needs presence, by a crisis that doesn't care about your content calendar — the loss isn't just professional. It's existential. Who are you when you are not producing?

Anabelle sat with that question. And then she sat with it again when caregiving and grief re-entered her life later, asking the same thing with even more force. The answer she arrived at is not tidy, but it is true: your value was never located in your output. It was always already there. The work just made it easier to avoid knowing that.

The Practical Work of Building a Sustainable Business

This episode doesn't stop at the emotional reckoning. Anabelle brings the conversation into concrete, actionable territory — because that's what The Digital Doula is actually built on: the belief that sustainable business requires both inner clarity and outer structure.

The one-week task audit she describes is deceptively simple. For seven days, you track every task you do and mark it honestly: does this energize you or drain you? Does it require you specifically, or could it live somewhere else? Most entrepreneurs who do this exercise are surprised by what they find — not that they're doing too much (they knew that), but by which tasks are costing the most and why they've held on to them.

Sometimes we keep doing the draining work because we're afraid of who we'll be without it. Delegation, then, isn't just an operational decision. It's an identity negotiation. And automation isn't a sign that you've stopped caring — it's a structural choice that protects the space where your best work, your deepest relationships, and your most creative thinking actually live.

A New Definition of Success

By the time Anabelle and Aimee reach the final stretch of this conversation, something has shifted. The question is no longer how to do more, faster, better. The question is what success actually looks like when you build it around a life instead of building it at the expense of one.

It's a quieter ambition than the one most of us were sold. It doesn't require you to be the person holding everything together. It asks you, instead, to build something that doesn't depend on that — a business with real structure, honest systems, and enough space inside it for the unexpected things that being a human being will inevitably bring you.

Anabelle Elya built that business after a pregnancy scare, after grief, after the kind of hard seasons that don't show up in highlight reels. And the question she leaves you with is the one worth carrying into your own work: what are you still doing because you believe everything depends on you?

This is the final conversation in the October Brand Builder Series. Watch Episode 84 with Amanda Carlson for more on founder friction and the businesses that still can't function without you at the center of everything.
